abstract.title: Significance
abstract.p: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is one of the most aggressive intracranial tumors for which there is no effective treatment. Here, we discussed the high proportion of GAM in gliomas, and demonstrated the extension of the median survival time in the GBM orthotopic mouse model by generating chimeric antigen receptor macrophage (CAR-M) in the tumor situ and reversal of tumor immunosuppressive microenvironment. Compared with lipid nanoparticles, the enucleated mesenchymal stem cells were utilized as vehicles for the targeted delivery of CAR-encoding plasmids to GAM, and specifically generated sufficient numbers of CAR-M in glioma situ to achieve GBM therapy. Moreover, this process altered the immune cell profiles within the tumor by increasing cytotoxic T cells and M1-like macrophages with antitumor activity.

Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is one of the most aggressive intracranial tumors for which there is no effective treatment. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophage (CAR-M) therapies have demonstrated impressive therapeutic efficacy in solid tumors; however, the cost and rigor associated with manufacturing engineered macrophages ex vivo can be prohibitive. Here, we utilized enucleated mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) as vehicles for the targeted delivery of CAR-encoding plasmid to reprogram glioma-associated microglia/macrophages (GAM), thereby achieving CAR-M preparation in vivo. Specifically, we observed that the enucleated cells retained the key organelle function and membrane integrity, and actively homed to glioma tissue. Interestingly, enucleated MSCs underwent intrinsic apoptosis due to the absence of the nucleus, which subsequently triggered macrophage-specific endocytosis, thereby achieving precise delivery of CAR-plasmids to GAM. Compared with lipid nanoparticles, this strategy specifically generated sufficient numbers of CAR-M in glioma situ to achieve GBM therapy. Moreover, this process altered the immune cell profiles within the tumor by increasing cytotoxic T cells and M1-like macrophages with antitumor activity. When combined with CD47-blocking therapies, tumor growth was completely suppressed in the GBM orthotopic mouse model, resulting in a 90-d survival rate of 83%. Collectively, our strategy provides a viable platform technology for CAR-M generation in vivo, which is expected to provide an approach for GBM therapy.

body.p: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is one of the most aggressive intracranial tumors (1, 2). Despite the significant advancements achieved in surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy over the past years, patients diagnosed with GBM still face a median survival of approximately 14 mo and a dismal 5-y survival rate of merely 4 to 5% after the first diagnosis (3, 4). Thus, effective therapeutic modalities for treating GBM are urgently needed.

In recent years, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has achieved great success in hematologic malignancies, but its application to solid tumors has been challenging (5). Unlike T cells, leveraging the exceptional tumor infiltration capacity and pleiotropic antitumor mechanisms (including phagocytosis and antigen presentation) of macrophages, CAR-M therapy is currently being evaluated in clinical trials worldwide (5, 6). Among them, HER2-targeted CAR-M therapy has demonstrated promising antitumor immune responses in patients with HER2-overexpressing relapsed/refractory solid tumors (7). In the GBM orthotopic mouse model, we also found that a single in situ infusion of CAR-M decreased tumor burden and prolonged overall survival. Unfortunately, the cost and rigor associated with manufacturing engineered macrophages ex vivo hinder their widespread application (8, 9). The limited proliferative capacity of primary macrophages has further hindered CAR-M progress toward clinical translation (10).

To address the abovementioned bottlenecks, we analyzed the complex composition of GBM and found that approximately 30 to 50% of the cells were microglia/macrophages, consistent with previous studies (11, 12). This fact raises the intriguing possibility that the glioma-associated microglia/macrophages (GAM) could be genetically engineered to generate CAR Ms in situ, thereby bypassing the need to extract and culture macrophages from patients to achieve GBM therapy. Based on this, the development of in situ CAR-M therapy necessitates efficient delivery of CAR plasmids to GAM within the tumor, which poses significant technical challenges. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) serve as an attractive vehicle for plasmid delivery due to their intrinsic tumor-homing capability (13, 14). However, critical challenges persist: Plasmids delivered via MSCs struggle to achieve effective release from cellular carriers and are difficult to redeliver to GAM after homing; in addition, the uncertain risk of proliferation, differentiation, and engraftment of living cells in the host also lead to unpredictable side effects, posing barriers to clinical application (15, 16).

Cell enucleation technology has been proven to preserve intact cell membrane structures while maintaining essential functions, including cellular migration and integrin-mediated adhesion (17–19). Meantime, this technique effectively eliminates cell proliferation capacity and tumorigenic risks (20, 21). Herein, we found that enucleated MSCs (eMSCs) still maintained the inherent tumor migration capacity after the removal of the nucleus. Given that cells cannot sustain long-term survival postnuclear deprivation, continuous monitoring revealed that eMSCs initiated programmed apoptosis following approximately 60 h of viability. This apoptotic process is characterized by phosphatidylserine (PS) externalization and surface exposure, generating a specific “eat-me” signal that facilitates efficient macrophage recognition. Leveraging this characteristic, we developed a glioma tissue-GAM cascade-targeted system that achieved precise delivery of CAR plasmids to GAM for in situ transfection: first, the retained tumor homing capability of eMSCs mediates targeted plasmid transport to glioma tissues; then, the programmed apoptosis induced by enucleation further promotes the intrinsic recognition of eMSCs by GAM, thereby driving secondary plasmid delivery into GAM for in situ transfection of CAR-M. Compared with systemic reinfusion of CAR-Ms, this in situ transfection strategy effectively mitigates concerns regarding potential autoimmune complications. Compared with lipid nanoparticles, this strategy specifically generated sufficient numbers of CAR-Ms in glioma situ, resulting in tumor regression. Moreover, this process altered the immune cell profiles within the tumor by increasing cytotoxic T cells and M1-like macrophages with antitumor activity. When combined with CD47-blocking therapies, tumor growth was completely suppressed in the GBM orthotopic mouse model, resulting in a 90-d survival rate of 83%. Collectively, our strategy provides a viable platform technology for CAR-M generation in vivo, which is expected to provide an approach for GBM therapy.

sec.title: A Single Intracranial Injection of CAR-Ms Inhibited the GBM Growth In Vivo.
sec.p: Recent evidence has suggested that CD133 (prominin-1, a pentaspan transmembrane glycoprotein) is highly expressed in GBM and promotes the metastasis of glioma cells (22–24). Further through bioinformatics analysis, CD133 mRNA expression levels were significantly higher in glioma tissues of patients with GBM (P < 0.01) than those in normal tissues (SI Appendix, Fig. S1A), which showed consistent results in the orthotopic GBM mouse models (SI Appendix, Fig. S1B). The optimum cut-off point for survival analysis was also established via log-rank testing on the PrognoScan platform, revealing that GBM patients with high CD133 expression exhibited poorer survival outcomes compared to those with low CD133 expression (HR = 1.28, COX P = 0.0133, SI Appendix, Fig. S1 C and D). Emerging evidence has established that CD133 is one of the potential therapeutic targets for GBM (25). Based on this, to determine the efficacy of the CAR-M strategy, we constructed CAR-Ms ex vivo containing the CD8α stalk and transmembrane domains, the CD3ζ domain, and the anti-CD133-scFv domain. We then administered a single intratumoral injection of 5 × 105 CAR-Ms to mice with established GL261 syngeneic gliomas (26). Bioluminescence from luciferase-gene has been shown to be positively correlated with tumor grade (27), so we used it to monitor tumor development at 7-d intervals following the initiation of treatment. Focusing on CAR-M groups, bioluminescence imaging throughout the treatment course revealed the pronounced antitumor effect (Fig. 1 A and B). Quantitative analysis performed on day 28 indicated that CAR-Ms achieved a tumor inhibition rate of 86.67%. Consistently, survival curves demonstrated that treatment with CAR-Ms significantly prolonged survival, with an above 80% survival rate within 100 d (Fig. 1C).

caption.p: A single intracranial injection of CAR-Ms inhibited the GBM growth in vivo. In vivo imaging (A) and graph (B) of orthotopic mouse models with luciferase-labeled glioma in the indicated treatment groups (n = 3; mean ± SD; two-way ANOVA). (C) Kaplan–Meier curves showing survival of mice treated with CAR-M and Control (n = 6; Log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test). Representative flow cytometry data of CD3+CD4+ (D) and CD3+CD8+ (E) subsets (gated on CD45+) in tumor tissues of mice treated with the different groups. ***P < 0.001; ****P < 0.0001.

sec.p: CAR-Ms exhibit both upregulation of costimulatory ligands and possess the established role of macrophages as professional antigen-presenting cells (28, 29). Given the abundant CAR-Ms transfused, investigating the effect of CAR-Ms on the surrounding the tumor microenvironment (TME) was warranted. Thus, we analyzed immune cells within the tumors on day 29 using flow cytometry. These results found that CAR-M therapy induced a polarization of macrophages toward an M1-like phenotype (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 A and B) and activation of CD4+ (Fig. 1D) and CD8+ (Fig. 1E) T cells within the TME. Furthermore, the injection of CAR-Ms increased the proportion of dendritic cells (DCs) (SI Appendix, Fig. S2C). These results provided initial evidence that CAR-Ms infusion was capable of remodeling the tumor immune microenvironment and enhancing antitumor therapy. To further confirm these in vivo observations, we assessed the impact of CAR-Ms in vitro and found that CAR Ms not only sustained the M1 phenotype but also inhibited the phenotype switching from M1 to M2 after coculture with tumor cells (SI Appendix, Fig. S3A). Additionally, this process enhanced the surface expression of MHC-II, indicating a role for CAR-Ms in antigen presentation (SI Appendix, Fig. S3B). Overall, CAR-M therapy presents a promising approach for GBM treatment, as it promotes phagocytosis and antigen processing.

sec.title: Analysis of Microglia/Macrophages in Glioblastoma and the Potential of Generated CAR-Ms In Vivo.
sec.p: Despite its remarkable therapeutic efficacy, the procedures for manufacturing autologous CAR-Ms ex vivo for the treatment of individual patients are complicated, and the proliferative capacity of primary macrophages is limited, thus posing challenges for broader clinical applications (9). During the tumorigenesis and progression of GBM, preclinical studies have revealed that glioma-infiltrating microglia/macrophages make up a large proportion of immune cells in GBM, and are associated with tumor grade (30–32). To further confirm the alterations, we found that the GAM marker ITGAM (integrin subunit alpha M) (Fig. 2A) and AIF-1 (allograft inflammatory factor-1) (SI Appendix, Fig. S4A) were highly expressed in glioma tissues of patients with GBM through bioinformatics analysis. The high infiltration status of GAM in GBM was also confirmed using the TIMER (Tumor Immune Estimation Resource) algorithm (Fig. 2B).

(A) The expression profiles of ITGAM genes in human glioblastoma within GEPIA (Gene Expression Profiling Interactive Analysis) database. The expression data are first log2 [transcripts per million (TPM)+1] transformed for differential analysis, and the log2FC is defined as median (tumor)–median (normal). *P < 0.01 was considered to be statistically significant. Statistical significance was analyzed by using the one-way ANOVA. The ratio of various cell populations in whole glioma tissues (Right, n = 5; mean ± SD). (D) Schematic illustration of the CAR-Ms generation in vivo by targeting GAM using enucleated MSCs as vehicles for the introduction of CAR-encoding plasmid.

sec.p: Meanwhile, we further confirmed the presence of GAM (F4/80+) (SI Appendix, Fig. S4B) in established glioma-bearing mice. Flow cytometry revealed that the GAM population accounted for more than 30% of total cells in the glioma, which was 40-fold higher than seen in age-matched healthy control mice (Fig. 2C and SI Appendix, Figs. S4C and S5). It was worth noting that about 65% of the GAM population were brain-intrinsic microglia. Based on these results, we hypothesize that in situ programmed CAR-Ms, which bypass the complex ex vivo preparation, have the potential to achieve effective GBM therapy. Here, we loaded CAR-encoding plasmids with enucleated MSCs to construct a plasmid delivery system. We demonstrated that, when administered in the presence of glioma, the enucleated MSCs vehicles with CAR-encoding plasmids could actively target the GAM within glioma, introducing CD133-specific CAR genes into the nuclei of GAM and inhibiting tumor growth (Fig. 2D).

sec.title: Enucleated MSCs Achieve Precise GAM Targeting in Glioblastoma.
sec.p: In fact, cell-based delivery vehicles, especially MSCs, could be designed for drug precise delivery through their natural chemotactic abilities (14, 33). However, such delivery systems faced the inability to control cell fate in vivo, such as by unpredictable engraftment as well as differentiation in the body, and even the risk of teratoma formation and malignant transformation of undifferentiated remnants, all of which notably limit predictable and reproducible therapeutic delivery (34, 35). Moreover, while cell-based delivery vehicles have shown potential for targeting specific tissues, achieving precise identification of target cells remains a significant challenge.

To render cell-based delivery vehicles safe and controllable, mouse adipose-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) were treated with cytochalasin B and further processed by Ficoll gradient ultracentrifugation to obtain enucleated MSCs (eMSCs) (Fig. 3A), according to the previously described methods (20, 36). By observing cellular morphology, the received eMSCs were readily attached to cell culture plates, and labeled via Actin-Tracker Red-555 and DAPI to mark the cell skeleton and nucleus, respectively. The results showed that there was no nucleus in the cytoplasm of eMSCs and possessed well-organized cytoskeletal structure (Fig. 3B). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was further utilized to confirm the successful removal of the nucleus in eMSCs (SI Appendix, Fig. S6A). Notably, various experiments have shown that eMSCs were substantially smaller than intact cells (Fig. 3 C and D and SI Appendix, Fig. S6B). It was worth noting that they also contained crucial subcellular organelles, including Golgi, endoplasmic reticulum (ER), mitochondria, lysosomes, and endosomes (SI Appendix, Fig. S6C) and had similar zeta potential as parental MSCs (SI Appendix, Fig. S6D). The western blot analysis revealed that eMSCs still conserved the proto-cell membrane markers CD105 (endoglin) as well as chemokine receptor CXCR4 (CXC motif chemokine receptor 4) (Fig. 3E); meanwhile, eMSCs sensed and migrated toward various chemo attractants in an in vitro transwell chamber assay (SI Appendix, Fig. S7A and Fig. 3F). Besides chemoattractant receptors, MSCs with endothelial adhesion molecules such as P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1 (PSGL-1) are another factor that can be targeted to the vasculature of diseased tissues, since they commonly express the ligands E- and P-selectin for PSGL-1. Flow cytometry showed that eMSCs retained stable surface expression of PSGL-1 for at least 24 h post enucleation (SI Appendix, Fig. S7B) and showed the ability to bind to P-/E-selectin (Fig. 3G), indicating the PSGL-1 on the surface of eMSCs was functional. Collectively, these results indicate that eMSCs retain critical cell structures, and possess the ability to activate chemotactic migration toward defined chemokine signals as well as to adhere to endothelial cells (Fig. 3H).

sec.p: Based on this, we next wanted to determine whether eMSCs administered i.v. can home to glioma tissue in vivo. To accomplish this, the near-infrared dye DiD was used as a probe and labeled the eMSCs or MSCs, and their biodistribution in glioma-bearing mice was tracked using an in vivo spectrum imaging system (IVIS). After intravenous administration, both cell types migrated rapidly, with large numbers having already entered the brain within 12 h, and the fluorescence signal in the brain continuing to increase, reaching a maximum at 48 h. Importantly, eMSCs showed substantially better homing compared with parental cells at all time points examined (Fig. 3 I and J and SI Appendix, Fig. S8A), which was probably due to facilitated systemic circulation mediated by cell volume reduction (37). Then, we dissected the brain at 72 h and evaluated the distribution of eMSCs or MSCs. Surprisingly, both MSCs and eMSCs were concentrated in the glioma tissue, while eMSCs showed a smaller punctate distribution and colocalized with GAM (Fig. 3K). Then, we further confirmed this phenomenon by flow cytometry analysis. The results showed that the fluorescence positive signal of eMSCs in immune cells was ~fourfold higher than that of MSCs, of which above 65% were GAM and only a small number of eMSCs was taken up by nonimmune cells (10.56 ± 2.03%) (Fig. 3L and SI Appendix, Fig. S8B). These results further confirmed the GAM targeting potential of enucleated MSCs in vivo.

Considering that the nuclei is an important and essential cell organelle required for cell survival, we tried to explore reasons for this phenomenon. As shown by the CCK 8 assay, eMSCs were viable for up to about 60 h post enucleation (SI Appendix, Fig. S9A). We further performed individual cell tracking, which showed that eMSCs appeared to die ultimately by apoptosis (Fig. 3M), and this speculation was further confirmed by examining the expression of the apoptosis-related proteins Caspase-3, Bcl-2, and Bax (Fig. 3N). Evidence suggests that apoptotic cell recognition and ingestion by macrophages is facilitated by PS displayed at the exofacial surface of the plasma membrane (38). We found that eMSCs could also trigger membrane translocation of PS during apoptosis (SI Appendix, Fig. S9B), which could possibly increase macrophage-mediated phagocytosis. Together, these findings demonstrate that, after spontaneous homing of eMSCs to the glioma site, apoptosis triggered by nuclear loss is sufficient to achieve precise targeting of GAM, thus laying the foundation for subsequent precise plasmid delivery (Fig. 3O).

sec.title: CAR Expression and Effector Activity of CAR-Ms In Vitro.
sec.p: Encouraged by the above findings, the enucleated MSCs were selected as vehicles for CAR-encoding plasmid delivery. To achieve efficient and stable loading of CAR plasmid (pCAR), Zn2+ and NLS (Nuclear localization sequence) peptides were utilized to prepare pCAR-containing nanoparticles (NP/pCAR), while optimizing the size and loading of the NLS peptides (SI Appendix, Fig. S10 A and B). Then, we obtained uniform and monodisperse NP/pCAR with a particle size of approximately 100 nm at a concentration of 100 μg/mL pCAR (Fig. 4A). The ability of NP/pCAR to load pCAR was confirmed by agarose gel electrophoresis (Fig. 4B). The change in zeta potential also demonstrated that NLS peptides and pCAR were successfully embedded in NP/pCAR (SI Appendix, Fig. S10C). Notably, the NP/pCAR was able to protect the plasmids from enzymatic degradation in the presence of DNase I, which was advantageous for the subsequent transfection (SI Appendix, Fig. S11). Subsequently, a pCAR delivery system based on eMSCs (eMSC/pCAR) was achieved by simple coincubation of the NP/pCAR with eMSCs, and maximum loading was achieved at a nanoparticle concentration of 200 μg/mL (SI Appendix, Fig. S12). Meanwhile, the confocal images showed that most pCAR were distributed in the cytoplasm of eMSCs and did not leak even during the occurrence of apoptosis (Fig. 4C).

sec.p: Multiple macrophage cells, including bone marrow–derived macrophages (BMDMs) and RAW 264.7 cells, were used to test the efficiency of eMSC/pCAR-mediated gene delivery. After incubation with the eMSC/pCAR, enhanced green fluorescent protein and anti-CD133-scFv on macrophages were measured using flow cytometry. As shown in Fig. 4D and SI Appendix, Fig. S13A, the percentage of CD133-scFv-positive macrophages in the eMSC/pCAR group was similar to the NP/pCAR group, and both were higher than those treated with free pCAR, indicating that the pCAR in eMSC/pCAR was sufficient for efficient transfection. The enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) expressed in the macrophages exhibited a similar trend (SI Appendix, Fig. S13 B and C). Next, we evaluated the CAR-mediated phagocytosis of macrophages on tumor cells through real-time tracking (Fig. 4E) and flow cytometry (Fig. 4F). In the eMSC/pCAR treatment group, the BMDMs gained a significant phagocytic capability compared with the free pCAR group. Meanwhile, the eMSC/pCAR-generated CARMs eradicated CD133+ GL261 in a dose and timedependent manner (Fig. 4G and SI Appendix, Fig. S14). These data suggested that the eMSC/pCAR engineered CAR macrophages had increased phagocytotic activity against CD133+ cancerous cells and provided support for further translation of this platform for macrophage reprogramming in vivo.

Since the tumor microenvironment makes the polarization balance of macrophages tend to M2 phenotype, we further used M2 BMDMs to investigate the phenotypic changes of CAR engineering. After coculture with tumor cells, the M2 marker CD206 was still significantly downregulated in eMSC/pCAR treated macrophages (SI Appendix, Fig. S15A). Meanwhile, the culture supernatants were collected to detect the secretion levels of inflammatory cytokines. The CD133+ fibroblasts were cocultured with eMSC/pCAR treated macrophages as controls. The results showed that CAR-engineered macrophages induced the most significant secretion of proinflammatory cytokines only when cocultured with CD133+ glioma cells, including IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β (Fig. 4H). In order to gain further insights into the biological changes induced by CAR signals, we distinguished macrophages based on successful (CAR+ M) and unsuccessful (CAR− M) CAR expression, and performed transcriptome analysis via RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) (Fig. 4I). As depicted in the Venn diagram and volcano plot, the intervention of CAR had a wide regulation for differential expressed genes (Fig. 4 J and K). We then analyzed the expression levels of genes, and found that genes related to inflammatory signaling and antigen processing and presentation were distinctly upregulated in the CAR+ M group compared to the control group. These changes were also observed in the CAR− M group, albeit to a lesser extent (Fig. 4L and SI Appendix, Fig. S15B). The pathway enrichment analyses demonstrated that CAR transduction led to the up-regulation of numerous markers associated with classically activated macrophages, including the inflammasome pathway, inducible regulation of toll-like receptor signaling pathway, interferon (IFN) signaling and NF-κB (nuclear factor kappa-B) signaling, consistent with classical proinflammatory macrophages (Fig. 4 M and N).

sec.title: Antitumor Efficacy of eMSC/pCAR in an Orthotopic Intracranial GBM Mouse Model.
sec.p: Recently, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery technology holds great potential as an efficient nonviral gene delivery vector due to its high gene transfection efficiency in vivo, which has been successfully used in clinical applications of gene therapy (39). For comparison, the modified lipid ratio was chosen to prepare LNP/pCAR as a control, which was demonstrated to possess an optimized formulation for efficient in vivo transfection (40, 41). The particle size of the obtained LNP/pCAR was 131.8 ± 37.13 nm (SI Appendix, Fig. S16), and the encapsulation efficiency was 92.10 ± 1.742%. Before evaluating the in vivo efficacy, we determined whether pCAR could reach the glioma via the intravenous route of administration. The established GL261 syngeneic glioma mice were randomly assigned to groups and administered equal amounts of Cy5-pCAR intravenously. At 12 h postinjection, a strong signal of Cy5 was clearly observed in the brain. More eMSC/pCAR migrated to the brain tissue as the time extended to 48 h, while the fluorescence in the LNP/pCAR group decreased gradually after 12 h (Fig. 5A). Meanwhile, after isolating the brain tissue at 72 h, eMSC/pCAR was partially colocalized with the infiltrating tumor signal and showed a significantly stronger signal than the LNP/pCAR group (~threefold) (Fig. 5 B and C).

(D) The experimental design to evaluate the antitumor efficacy by eMSC/pCAR. (J) Quantitative analysis of CD133+ cancer cells retained in the tumor tissues after treatment with eMSCs, LNP/pCAR, or eMSC/pCAR using flow cytometry (n = 3; one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test). (K) Kaplan–Meier survival curves of each group (n = 6; Log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test). The results are shown as the mean ± SD (A, C, F, and J). **P < 0.01; ***P < 0.001; ****P < 0.0001.

sec.p: Encouraged by the above results, we examined the therapeutic potential of eMSC/pCAR in the established GL261 glioma mouse model. Codelivery of pCAR and hyperactive insect piggyBac transposase with a seven–amino acid substitution (iPB7) with the eMSC/pCAR efficiently reprogrammed peritumoral glioma-associated macrophages to express CD133-targeted CAR in vivo. Eight days after inoculation with Luci+ GL261 cells, various preparations were injected intravenously for 3 consecutive days. The dose of eMSC/pCAR was 2.5 × 106 cells per mouse, and the control group was given equal doses of pCAR (Fig. 5D). Throughout the treatment course, bioluminescence imaging revealed that eMSC/pCAR groups conferred the strongest antitumor effect, and significantly higher than the LNP/pCAR group (Fig. 5 E and F). The brain tissues were harvested on day 29 after inoculation, and tumor-bearing brain slices stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL). Mice treated with eMSC/pCAR showed the most pronounced tumor damage and cell apoptosis, while the therapeutic effects of eMSCs could be ignored (Fig. 5 G and H). Meanwhile, we analyzed cells that retained CD133 expression in tumors and found that eMSC/pCAR reduced the mean fluorescence intensity of CD133+ cancer cells and inhibited proliferation in vivo (Fig. 5 I and J). Consistently, the survival curves showed that treatment with eMSC/pCAR markedly increased survival rates to a median of 57 d, significantly longer than those achieved with PBS (36 d) (Fig. 5K). We also noted that the body weight in eMSC/pCAR-treated mice showed almost no change (about 20.0 g) within 20 d, while the body weight in other groups was rapidly decreased within a few days (SI Appendix, Fig. S17).

sec.title: In Vivo Expression Analysis of CAR and Tumor Microenvironment Remodeling.
sec.p: Next, we further analyzed the timing of CAR-M production in vivo during the antitumor process, and the transfection efficiency of CAR in brain tissues was determined with EGFP fluorescence. The study revealed that macrophages underwent rapid and efficient reprogramming in vivo from days 6 to 15, with sustained high-level CAR transgene expression (23.67 ± 2.91%) maintained at day 15 (SI Appendix, Fig. S18A). Then, the expression and specificity of CAR after treatment were also detected by IVIS and flow cytometry, respectively (Fig. 6A). As shown in Fig. 6B, the large area of EGFP fluorescence expression near the tumor in the eMSC/pCAR group was significantly stronger than that in the LNP/pCAR group. Notably, the percentages of EGFP fluorescence-positive T cells, DCs, neutrophils, and tumor cells in glioma tissue were negligible (Fig. 6C and SI Appendix, Fig. S18B). The transfection specificity may be attributed to the specific targeting of macrophages by eMSCs-mediated apoptosis. In parallel experiments, we performed tissue section analysis of brain tissue. As shown in Fig. 6D and SI Appendix, Fig. S18C, EGFP fluorescence was gathered in and around the tumor, and a large number of them were GAM. It is worth noting that colocalization of CD133 and EGFP fluorescence was observed in CAR macrophages, confirming that the eMSC/pCAR treatment resulted in specific phagocytosis of CD133+ cancer cells by macrophages.

(C) The percentages of EGFP fluorescence-positive macrophages, T cells, neutrophils, tumor cells, and DCs after treated with LNP/pCAR or eMSC/pCAR using flow cytometry (n = 3; two-way ANOVA). The CD133+ tumor cell, GAM, and nucleus are labeled by CD133 (yellow), F4/80 (red), and DAPI (blue), respectively. (Scale bar, Left image, 500 μm; Right enlarged image, 50 μm.) The results are shown as the mean ± SD (C, E–G, and I). ns, no significant difference; ****P < 0.0001.

sec.p: Following confirmation that GAM could be specifically transfected by eMSC/pCAR in vivo, we next examined their effects on the TME. We analyzed immune cells in the tumors using flow cytometry and observed a significant increase in activated CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells in the tumors of eMSC/pCAR treated mice (Fig. 6E and SI Appendix, Fig. S19 A and B). The population of M1 macrophages in the tumor of the mice in the eMSC/pCAR group was ~fourfold higher than that in the control group; meanwhile, an opposite trend occurred for M2 macrophages (Fig. 6F and SI Appendix, Fig. S19 C and D). The population of DCs in the eMSC/pCAR group was also higher than that in the control group (Fig. 6G and SI Appendix, Fig. S19E). The secretion of M1 macrophage–related cytokines in tumor, including IFN-γ, IL-12, and TNF-α, was elevated after treatment with eMSC/pCAR (Fig. 6H). These findings collectively revealed that eMSC/pCAR treatment selectively generated CAR-Ms in vivo and conferred potent tumor-killing immunity in tumor tissues. Meanwhile, the factor levels in the serum exhibited a mild elevation followed by gradual resolution during the treatment phase (Fig. 6I). However, these values remained substantially below pathological thresholds (42), thereby affirming the safety of the factor levels in vivo.

sec.title: Combined eMSC/pCAR and CD47 Blockade Enhances Glioma-Killing Efficacy.
sec.p: Accumulating evidence indicates that tumor cells evade immune recognition by upregulating the “don’t eat me” transmembrane protein CD47 (43, 44). Bioinformatics analysis revealed significantly elevated mRNA levels of both CD133 and CD47 in GBM tissues compared to normal brain tissues (SI Appendix, Figs. S1A and S20A), a finding corroborated by elevated protein expression in orthotopic GBM mouse models (Fig. 7A and SI Appendix, Fig. S20B). Based on these observations, we investigated the synergistic antitumor efficacy of combining CD47 blockade with the eMSC/pCAR strategy. Glioma-bearing mice received intratumoral injection of anti-CD47 on day 8 after tumor inoculation. The other treatments were tested using the same time course, and eMSC/pCAR loaded with empty plasmid vector (eMSC/Vector) was used as control. As shown in Fig. 7 B and C and SI Appendix, Fig. S21, anti-CD47 (aCD47) monotherapy partially reduced the tumor burden; notably, the combination therapy group exhibited an approximately 4.2-fold reduction in bioluminescence intensity compared to the aCD47 monotherapy group at day 28, along with significantly prolonged survival (Fig. 7D). These findings validated the synergistic tumor-suppressive effects of the combination therapy. H&E and TUNEL staining of tumor tissue exhibited a similar trend (Fig. 7 E and F). Meanwhile, the combination treatment group exhibited the lowest levels of target cell antigen expression in the tumor tissue (Fig. 7G); there was an elevation in the secretion of proinflammatory factors in tumor (Fig. 7H). These data demonstrated that codelivery of eMSC/pCAR and anti-CD47 achieved the most robust antitumor efficacy.

(B) Time-dependent tumor burden was determined by bioluminescent imaging at the indicated days (n = 3). (C) Quantification of bioluminescent signal analyses on day 28 (n = 3; mean ± SD; one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test). (D) Kaplan–Meier survival curves of each group (n = 6; Log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test). H&E (E, Scale bars, 2 mm) and TUNEL (F, Scale bars, 100 μm) staining of the brain tissue from each group. (G) Representative images of tumor tissue stained with CD133 and Ki67. (Scale bars, 100 μm.) (H) Representative immuno-fluorescence staining for IL-2, IFN-γ, and TNF-α in tumor tissues. (Scale bar, 100 μm.) ns, no significant difference; ***P < 0.001. ****P < 0.0001.

sec.p: Encouraged by the above results, we further validated the therapeutic efficacy in the CT2A syngeneic glioma model to demonstrate the broad applicability of our therapeutic strategy (26). We established orthotopic CT2A glioma-bearing mice and randomly divided them into four groups on day 9 postinjection. Bioluminescence imaging throughout the treatment course revealed that the combination therapy group showed the strongest antitumor effect (SI Appendix, Fig. S22A). Quantitative analysis on day 30 showed that the combination therapy group exhibited an approximately 7.03-fold reduction in bioluminescence intensity compared to the anti-CD47 antibody monotherapy group, and an approximately 4.32-fold reduction compared to the eMSC/pCAR group (SI Appendix, Fig. S22B). Consistently, H&E staining and TUNEL assay further confirmed that the combination therapy group exhibited a significant reduction in tumor area (SI Appendix, Fig. S22C) and a marked increase in tumor cells death (SI Appendix, Fig. S22D) compared to the control group. These results confirmed that the antitumor effects of this treatment modality might be universally applicable to GBM therapy.

Based on the therapeutic responses we achieve, we next assessed whether eMSC/pCAR was biocompatible and safe for repeated dosing. Healthy mice were injected with a total of three doses of eMSC/pCAR, which was consistent with the treatment cycle. They were killed 21 d after the infusion, blood was collected by retro-orbital bleed for serum chemistry. The body temperature changes following the initial eMSC/pCAR dose. We noticed a significant ~1 to 2 °C rise in body temperature 30 min after treatment (SI Appendix, Fig. S23A). Following all subsequent injections, body temperature remained normal (SI Appendix, Fig. S23 B and C). Meanwhile, serum chemistry of eMSC/pCAR-treated mice was comparable to that of PBS, indicating that systemic toxicities did not occur (SI Appendix, Fig. S24). Following injection of eMSC/pCAR, we measured moderate changes in serum levels of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β (SI Appendix, Fig. S25). Based on previous reports, these levels are much lower than those associated with pathological findings and thus can be considered safe (42). Taken together, these results indicate eMSC/pCAR are biocompatible and safe for repeated intravenous dosing.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: GBM is the most aggressive brain tumor type in humans. There is no fully effective therapy, and chemotherapy or radiotherapy is still the major strategy for GBM clinical treatment (2, 45). Therefore, treatment for GBM remains a serious clinical and scientific problem. Here, we discussed the high proportion of GAM in gliomas (approximately 30 to 50%), and the extension of the median survival time from 36 to 57 d in the GBM orthotopic mouse model by generating CAR Ms in the tumor situ and restructuring the TME. Importantly, combined with CD47-blocking therapies, tumor growth was completely suppressed, resulting in a 90-d survival rate of 83%.

Achieving efficient in vivo gene delivery to target cells is difficult. Currently, the attempts have mainly focused on the use of traditional technologies (e.g., LNP) loaded with target genes for CAR-Ms production in vivo (46, 47). However, designing methods with macrophage tropism and intracellular delivery efficacy using traditional technologies is challenging. Cellular enucleation, a classic technique in cell biology, involves the separation of the nucleus from the cytoplasm and finally generating a nucleus-free cytoplast (18, 36). Additionally, enucleated cells are incapable of carrying out gene transcription, which means they cannot be stimulated to differentiate or produce unforeseeable cytokines in vivo (19, 21). Based on this advantage, we prepared enucleated MSCs as vehicles. Interestingly, we found that it could achieve specific macrophage targeting in vivo. The core of this system involves inducing spontaneous cell apoptosis in vivo by removing the nucleus of MSCs. Compared with lipid nanoparticles, this vehicle specifically generated sufficient numbers of CAR-Ms in glioma situ (∼fivefold), resulting in tumor regression. Notably, our approach patently contrasts with those currently used to generate macrophages with defined specificities against tumors, which require isolation of macrophages from the patient’s blood and their genetic modification via complex laboratory procedures based on viral vectors.

At this point, it is not difficult to predict the ways the approach we describe here could also be used to develop injectable medicine configured to treat beyond cancer therapy for a wide range of disease types that macrophages play key roles in the pathogenesis, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis (48).

In summary, these findings establish that our strategy selectively generated CAR-Ms in vivo and conferred potent tumor-killing immunity in tumor tissues. Notably, this delivery method is safe for repeated dosing, with only modest increases in the expression levels of inflammatory cytokines. Therefore, our work may overcome limitations of traditional treatment methods and provide a strategy to solve the treatment problems of GBM, warranting further clinical validation.

sec.title: Animal.
sec.p: The C57BL/6 mice (SPF class) were purchased from the Spelford Laboratory Animal Centre (Beijing, China). All animals were fed in the condition of 25 °C and 55% relative humidity in the Experimental Animal Center of Zhengzhou University. All mice were maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions with a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle.

sec.title: Cell Culture.
sec.p: Murine adipose-derived MSCs were purchased from Wanwu Biotechnology Inc. (Hefei, China). The RAW 264.7 cell line, GL261 luciferase-positive cell line (Luci+ GL261), and 3T3-L1 cell line were purchased from the Sunncell Bioscience Inc. (Wuhan, China). CT2A luciferase-positive cell line (Luci+ CT2A) was purchased from Xyzcell Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). All cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Procell), and a 5% CO2 atmosphere at 37 °C. Bone marrow–derived macrophages (BMDMs) were isolated from mouse femurs and cultured in DMEM containing 20% FBS, 1% penicillin/streptomycin, and 20 ng/mL M-CSF ex vivo for 7 d under 5% CO2 atmosphere at 37 °C. All cells were negative for mycoplasma contamination.
We refer the readers to SI Appendix for full, detailed description of all the methods used in this study.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism. The methods of applying statistical analysis and definition of statistically significant findings can be found in SI Appendix.

Afterward, the glioma cells (red) were co-incubated (at a ratio of BMDM vs to GL261 cells at 4:1). The phagocytosis process was recorded and images were taken for the dual channel.
